profile.Assumption: LPN with constant noise rate and uniform matrix, hard for polynomial-time adversaries

metadata.resolution_condition: An IND-CPA secure public-key encryption scheme (or two-message key agreement) with negligible decryption error whose security reduces with polynomial loss to decisional or search LPN with a uniformly random matrix, polynomially many samples, and some constant noise rate 0 < μ < 1/2, assuming hardness only against polynomial-time adversaries. Schemes from sparse, dense-sparse or sparse-secret LPN variants, schemes at noise rate O(1/√n), and schemes that need 2^ω(√n) hardness do not count.
metadata.summary: Can public-key encryption be based on learning parity with noise at a constant noise rate, assuming hardness only against polynomial-time adversaries? Known schemes need noise about \( 1/\sqrt{n} \) or sub-exponential hardness of constant-noise LPN.
metadata.title: Public-key encryption from constant-noise LPN

sections.content:
Learning parity with noise (LPN) asks to recover a secret
\( s \in \mathbb{F}_2^n \) from noisy linear equations
\( \langle a_i, s \rangle + e_i \) with uniformly random \( a_i \) and
Bernoulli noise \( e_i \) of rate \( \mu \); at constant \( \mu \) it is a
standard assumption from which private-key cryptography follows. Public-key
encryption from LPN, starting with PKE-PAPER-2003-ALEKHNOVICH, is known under
polynomial hardness only at noise rate about \( 1/\sqrt{n} \), because
decryption must cancel an inner product of two noise vectors, and that inner
product is biased only at such low noise (PKE-PAPER-2016-YZ). Whether
constant-noise LPN alone yields public-key encryption is a basic feasibility
question about where this assumption sits.
sections.heading: Background

sections.content:
Construct an IND-CPA secure public-key encryption scheme with negligible
decryption error whose security reduces, with polynomial loss, to decisional
LPN with a constant noise rate \( 0 < \mu < 1/2 \), a uniformly random dense
matrix and polynomially many samples, assuming hardness only against
polynomial-time adversaries. Two-message key agreement with the same
properties is equivalent.
sections.heading: Problem

sections.content:
The Alekhnovich template, used by PKE-PAPER-2003-ALEKHNOVICH and
PKE-PAPER-2014-KMP, publishes \( (A, As + e) \) and decrypts through an inner
product in which two noise vectors meet; correctness needs this inner product
to be biased, which holds only for noise rate \( O(1/\sqrt{n}) \). This is why
[the low-noise case](PKE-OP-003) is settled while [a noise rate polynomially
above the square-root threshold](PKE-OP-005) is already open.
PKE-PAPER-2016-YZ avoid the template's limit by showing that constant-noise
LPN stays secure when the secret has only polylogarithmic entropy, which costs
the assumption that LPN is \( 2^{\omega(n^{1/2})} \)-hard, and so obtain
[public-key encryption from sub-exponentially hard constant-noise
LPN](PKE-OP-004). PKE-PAPER-2021-YZ note that this hardness level is almost
what worst-case nearest-codeword reductions provide, and leave open whether
the gap closes. Other schemes change the assumption to sparse noisy equations
(PKE-PAPER-2010-ABW) or Dense-Sparse LPN (PKE-PAPER-2024-DJ); these variants
are not known to be implied by standard LPN, so they settle different
questions. No separation specific to LPN is known, so the obstacle is a
limitation of current techniques.
sections.heading: Why it is open

sections.content:
- Schemes from sparse LPN, Dense-Sparse LPN, sparse-secret LPN, LPN over
  larger fields or rings, or LWE.
- Schemes that need \( 2^{\omega(\sqrt{n})} \)-hardness of constant-noise LPN,
  which PKE-PAPER-2016-YZ already provide.
- Schemes at noise rate \( O(1/\sqrt{n}) \), or heuristic constructions
  without a reduction to LPN.
sections.heading: What would not resolve it

sections.content:
For \( n = \mathrm{poly}(\lambda) \), \( m = \mathrm{poly}(n) \) and a constant
\( \mu \in (0, 1/2) \), let \( \mathrm{LPN}_{n,\mu,m} \) be the problem of
distinguishing \( (A, As + e) \) from \( (A, u) \), where
\( A \leftarrow \mathbb{F}_2^{m \times n} \), \( s \leftarrow \mathbb{F}_2^{n} \),
\( e \leftarrow \mathrm{Ber}(\mu)^{m} \) and \( u \leftarrow \mathbb{F}_2^{m} \)
are uniform or Bernoulli as indicated. The target is a public-key encryption
scheme with decryption error \( \mathrm{negl}(\lambda) \) and a reduction
\( \mathcal{R} \) such that, for every probabilistic polynomial-time IND-CPA
adversary \( \mathcal{A} \), the algorithm \( \mathcal{R}^{\mathcal{A}} \) runs
in polynomial time and

\[
\mathrm{Adv}^{\mathrm{IND\text{-}CPA}}(\mathcal{A})
\le \mathrm{poly}(\lambda) \cdot \mathrm{Adv}^{\mathrm{LPN}_{n,\mu,m}}(\mathcal{R}^{\mathcal{A}}) + \mathrm{negl}(\lambda).
\]
sections.heading: Formal target

sections.content:
PKE-PAPER-2016-YZ observe that noise rate \( O(1/\sqrt{n}) \) seems an
inherent barrier to correctness for the Alekhnovich-type scheme, and
PKE-PAPER-2010-ABW note that known schemes from dense LPN and LWE all require
noise below \( 1/\sqrt{m} \). These are limitations of known designs, not
lower bounds. No black-box separation between constant-noise LPN and
public-key encryption is known; generic separations between one-way functions
and key agreement do not apply, because a construction may use the linear
structure of LPN rather than its one-wayness alone.
sections.heading: Known obstacles

sections.content:
PKE-PAPER-2003-ALEKHNOVICH gave the first LPN-type public-key encryption, at
noise rate below \( 1/\sqrt{n} \). PKE-PAPER-2010-ABW obtained public-key
encryption from sparse noisy equations at higher noise. Chosen-ciphertext
security followed in the low-noise regime, including the simple construction
of PKE-PAPER-2014-KMP, whose authors listed constant noise as open.
PKE-PAPER-2016-YZ reached constant noise under sub-exponential hardness,
PKE-PAPER-2021-YZ related that hardness level to worst-case nearest-codeword
problems, and PKE-PAPER-2024-DJ obtained lossy trapdoor functions from
Dense-Sparse LPN at inverse-polynomial noise.

metadata.resolution_condition: A verified proof that, for every δ-correct randomized PKE and FO with implicit rejection (FO^⊥̸ or FO^⊥̸_m in the notation of HHK17), every QROM IND-CCA adversary making q random-oracle queries yields an IND-CPA adversary of comparable running time with Adv^IND-CCA ≤ c · Adv^IND-CPA + statistical terms, for an absolute constant c. Statistical conditions with explicit error terms (for example η-injectivity) are allowed; additional computational or structural assumptions on the PKE (disjoint simulatability, unique randomness recoverability, lossy or parameter-lossy keys) are not. A proof whose IND-CPA term carries a factor growing with q or with the query depth does not close the problem.
metadata.summary: Can IND-CCA security of a Fujisaki–Okamoto KEM be reduced in the quantum random oracle model to IND-CPA security of the underlying scheme with only a constant-factor loss? Known reductions lose a square root or a polynomial factor in the oracle queries.
metadata.title: Tight QROM security of Fujisaki–Okamoto KEMs from IND-CPA

sections.content:
Post-quantum KEMs such as ML-KEM (PKE-PAPER-2024-FIPS203) obtain
chosen-ciphertext security by applying a variant of the Fujisaki–Okamoto (FO)
transform (PKE-PAPER-1999-FO) to a passively secure encryption scheme, and
their proofs must hold in the quantum random oracle model (QROM), where the
adversary may query the hash functions in superposition. A reduction is tight
when the KEM's IND-CCA advantage is at most a constant multiple of an IND-CPA
advantage against the underlying scheme, up to statistical terms. A square
root or a factor in the number of oracle queries means that parameters chosen
from the underlying hard problem carry a weaker proven guarantee for the KEM.
sections.heading: Background

sections.content:
Let PKE be a randomized public-key encryption scheme with correctness error
\( \delta \), and let the KEM be FO with implicit rejection, in either the
\( \mathrm{FO}^{\not\bot} \) or the \( \mathrm{FO}^{\not\bot}_m \) form of
PKE-PAPER-2017-HHK. Is there a QROM reduction that turns any IND-CCA adversary
against the KEM, making \( q \) quantum random-oracle queries and classical
decapsulation queries, into an IND-CPA adversary against PKE with comparable
running time, such that the IND-CCA advantage is at most an absolute constant
times the IND-CPA advantage plus statistical terms? No square root and no
factor growing with \( q \) or with the query depth may multiply the IND-CPA
advantage, and no assumption on PKE beyond IND-CPA and stated statistical
conditions may be used.
sections.heading: Problem

sections.content:
In the classical random oracle model a reduction can read the adversary's
queries and use the one that encrypts the challenge, which gives [tight
classical proofs](PKE-OP-006). In the QROM the queries are quantum, and the
one-way-to-hiding lemmas used instead traditionally cost a square root, so
[the first proofs without ciphertext overhead](PKE-OP-008) lost a square root
and a factor in the number of queries (PKE-PAPER-2018-JZCWM).
PKE-PAPER-2021-JZM shows that for perfectly correct schemes the square root is
unavoidable for black-box reductions that run the adversary once and measure
one of its oracle queries. The proofs of PKE-PAPER-2020-KSSSS and
PKE-PAPER-2024-GLX leave that class by rewinding a unitary adversary and
reach [square-root-free security](PKE-OP-007), but pay polynomial factors in
the query depth; a 2026 preprint, PKE-PAPER-2026-GYY, claims to lower the
query factor to \( O(\sqrt{q}) \). Tightness is known only when the
underlying scheme has extra structure, such as [parameter-lossy
keys](PKE-OP-009) (PKE-PAPER-2023-PWZ).
sections.heading: Why it is open

sections.content:
- Tight proofs that add assumptions on the encryption scheme: disjoint
  simulatability, unique randomness recoverability, or lossy or
  parameter-lossy keys.
- Tight reductions for the deterministic KEM step alone from OW-CPA: FO must
  also handle the derandomization of a randomized scheme.
- Proofs in the classical random oracle model, where tightness from IND-CPA
  is already known.
- Better statistical terms (correctness error, spreadness) that leave the
  factor on the IND-CPA advantage unchanged.
sections.heading: What would not resolve it

sections.content:
Let \( \mathrm{PKE} = (\mathrm{KG}, \mathrm{Enc}, \mathrm{Dec}) \) have
message space \( \mathcal{M} \), randomness space \( \mathcal{R} \) and
correctness error \( \delta \). With random oracles
\( G : \mathcal{M} \to \mathcal{R} \) and \( H \), the KEM
\( \mathrm{FO}^{\not\bot}[\mathrm{PKE}, G, H] \) encapsulates by sampling
\( m \leftarrow \mathcal{M} \), setting \( c = \mathrm{Enc}(pk, m; G(m)) \)
and \( K = H(m, c) \); decapsulation re-encrypts the decrypted message and,
on mismatch or failure, returns a key derived from a secret seed and \( c \)
(implicit rejection). In the QROM, let \( \mathcal{A} \) make \( q \)
quantum queries to \( G \) and \( H \) and \( q_D \) classical decapsulation
queries. The target is an IND-CPA adversary \( \mathcal{B} \) with
\( \mathrm{Time}(\mathcal{B}) \le \mathrm{poly}(\mathrm{Time}(\mathcal{A})) \)
and

\[
\mathrm{Adv}^{\mathrm{IND\text{-}CCA}}_{\mathrm{FO}^{\not\bot}[\mathrm{PKE},G,H]}(\mathcal{A})
\le c \cdot \mathrm{Adv}^{\mathrm{IND\text{-}CPA}}_{\mathrm{PKE}}(\mathcal{B})
+ \mathrm{poly}(q, q_D) \cdot \delta
+ \frac{\mathrm{poly}(q)}{|\mathcal{M}|}
+ \mathrm{Adv}^{\mathrm{PRF}}
\]

for an absolute constant \( c \) (statistical injectivity or spreadness
terms with explicit error may be added). A multi-user, multi-challenge
version, whose loss must also be independent of the numbers of users and
challenge ciphertexts, is a further strengthening.
sections.heading: Formal target

sections.content:
PKE-PAPER-2021-JZM prove, for perfectly correct schemes, that a black-box
reduction which runs the adversary once without rewinding, measures the input
of one of its random-oracle queries, and post-processes the outcome reaches
only about the square of the adversary's advantage; simple sequential
rewinding does not help. This rules out square-root-free proofs within that
class only. It says nothing about factors polynomial in \( q \), about
reductions that rewind by inverting the adversary's quantum operations (as in
PKE-PAPER-2020-KSSSS and PKE-PAPER-2024-GLX), or about schemes with extra
structure. The rewinding proofs in turn treat the adversary as a unitary
algorithm, which costs space linear in its running time
(PKE-PAPER-2024-GLX, Remark 5).
sections.heading: Known obstacles

sections.content:
PKE-PAPER-2017-HHK gave the modular FO analysis with tight classical proofs
and highly non-tight QROM proofs, and asked for tighter ones.
PKE-PAPER-2018-JZCWM gave QROM proofs for implicit rejection without
ciphertext overhead and identified a tight reduction from IND-CPA as an
important open problem. PKE-PAPER-2019-BHHHP removed the query factor with a
double-sided one-way-to-hiding lemma but kept the square root, and
PKE-PAPER-2021-JZM explained why measurement-based reductions must keep it.
PKE-PAPER-2020-KSSSS introduced measure-rewind-measure to remove the square
root at a polynomial cost, and PKE-PAPER-2024-GLX lowered that cost and

metadata.title: Chosen-ciphertext security from any CPA-secure encryption

sections.content:
Chosen-plaintext (IND-CPA) security hides messages from an adversary that
sees only the public key and ciphertexts; chosen-ciphertext (IND-CCA2)
security must hold even when the adversary may decrypt any ciphertext other
than the challenge. IND-CCA2 is the standard requirement for deployed
encryption, and many schemes achieve it from specific assumptions, such as
PKE-PAPER-1998-CS under decisional Diffie–Hellman and a hash assumption. In
the random oracle model the Fujisaki–Okamoto transform builds it from any
passively secure scheme (PKE-PAPER-1999-FO), but in the standard model it is
not known whether IND-CPA security alone suffices (PKE-PAPER-2024-HDV).
sections.heading: Background

sections.content:
Is there a construction, black-box or not, that turns any IND-CPA secure
public-key encryption scheme into an IND-CCA2 secure one, with a
standard-model proof that assumes nothing beyond the IND-CPA security of the
given scheme? PKE-PAPER-2024-HDV state the black-box form as a major open
problem.
sections.heading: Problem

sections.content:
With a random oracle the answer is positive ([the random-oracle
case](PKE-OP-011)): the transform derives encryption coins from a hash and
re-encrypts during decryption to reject malformed ciphertexts. In the
standard model, PKE-PAPER-2007-GMM show that no black-box construction is
secure if its decryption never calls the underlying encryption algorithm,
and this holds already for [non-adaptive chosen-ciphertext
security](PKE-OP-013) (PKE-PAPER-2007-GMM, §1.2 and Theorem 26). PKE-PAPER-2024-HDV extend the
separation to quantum adversaries and reductions. Positive results either
[bound the number of decryption queries](PKE-OP-012) in advance
(PKE-PAPER-2006-CHK) or add a building block, such as [one-time
key-dependent-message secure secret-key encryption](PKE-OP-014)
(PKE-PAPER-2019-KMT), so [obtaining that block from IND-CPA
alone](PKE-OP-015) would suffice.
sections.heading: Why it is open

sections.content:
- Transforms in the random oracle model, such as Fujisaki–Okamoto.
- Constructions that add a further primitive or assumption: non-interactive
  zero-knowledge proofs, hinting pseudorandom generators, key-dependent-message
  secure encryption, lossy or injective trapdoor functions, or specific
  number-theoretic or lattice assumptions.
- Security for a number of decryption queries fixed in advance, or
  non-malleability under chosen-plaintext attack only.
sections.heading: What would not resolve it

sections.content:
Given black-box or code access to any public-key encryption scheme
\( \Pi = (\mathsf{KG}, \mathsf{Enc}, \mathsf{Dec}) \) that is IND-CPA secure
against probabilistic polynomial-time adversaries, construct
\( \Pi' = (\mathsf{KG}', \mathsf{Enc}', \mathsf{Dec}') \) and a reduction
showing that every adversary with advantage \( \varepsilon \) in the IND-CCA2
game against \( \Pi' \), which may query \( \mathsf{Dec}' \) on any ciphertext
other than the challenge before and after receiving it, yields an IND-CPA
adversary against \( \Pi \) with advantage
\( \varepsilon / \mathrm{poly}(\lambda) - \mathrm{negl}(\lambda) \). No random
oracle, common reference string, or assumption other than the IND-CPA security
of \( \Pi \) may be used.
sections.heading: Formal target

sections.content:
The black-box separation of PKE-PAPER-2007-GMM rules out shielding
constructions, those whose decryption does not call
the encryption algorithm of the given scheme, even for non-adaptive
chosen-ciphertext security. It does not rule out constructions that
re-encrypt during decryption, or non-black-box constructions.
PKE-PAPER-2024-HDV show that allowing quantum adversaries and reductions does
not help shielding constructions. PKE-PAPER-2006-CHK point out that, by the
result of PKE-PAPER-2007-GMM, black-box constructions are also impossible
when the bound on decryption queries depends only on the adversary.
sections.heading: Known obstacles

sections.content:
PKE-PAPER-1999-FO gave the random-oracle answer. PKE-PAPER-2006-CHK obtained
security for a number of decryption queries fixed at key generation from any
IND-CPA scheme, and PKE-PAPER-2007-GMM proved the shielding separation.
PKE-PAPER-2019-KMT reduced the question to a weak form of key-dependent-message
security for secret-key encryption, and PKE-PAPER-2024-HDV carried the
separation to the post-quantum setting, restating the question as a major open
problem.

In the random oracle model, turn any IND-CPA secure public-key encryption

sections.heading: Problem

sections.content:
PKE-PAPER-1999-FO combine a one-way asymmetric scheme with a one-time secure
symmetric scheme: the symmetric key is a hash of a random seed, the seed is
encrypted asymmetrically with coins hashed from the seed and the symmetric
ciphertext, and decryption re-encrypts to reject malformed ciphertexts. The
result is IND-CCA2 in the random oracle model, under a mild spreadness
condition on the asymmetric scheme. IND-CPA security with a large message
space implies one-wayness, and one-time symmetric encryption follows from
one-way functions; PKE-PAPER-2024-HDV cite this line of transforms as the
positive answer in the random oracle model. Its decryption calls the
encryption algorithm, which is what the standard-model separation of
PKE-PAPER-2007-GMM requires of any black-box construction.

Construct IND-CCA secure public-key encryption from an IND-CPA secure
public-key encryption scheme and a secret-key encryption scheme that stays
secure when it encrypts, once, a projection of its own key, that is, a string
each of whose bits is a constant, a bit of the key, or the negation of a bit of

sections.heading: Problem

sections.content:
PKE-PAPER-2019-KMT give this construction, fully black-box, for secret-key
encryption that can encrypt plaintexts of length \( \Omega(n\lambda) \) for key
length \( n \) (Theorem 2 and Corollary 1). Because projection-KDM-secure
public-key encryption yields both building blocks, it also implies IND-CCA
secure public-key encryption (Corollary 2). Decryption re-runs the encryption
algorithm of the underlying scheme, and this is necessary: no black-box
construction from projection-KDM-secure encryption whose decryption avoids it
reaches even IND-CCA1 security (Theorem 4). The same approach gives trapdoor
functions with adaptive one-wayness, including one from sub-exponentially hard
constant-noise LPN.

sections.content: Towards a Separation of Semantic and CCA Security for Public Key Encryption
sections.heading: Overview

sections.content: The conference version appears at TCC 2007. The ePrint full version, headed "Extended Abstract" but 77 pages with the full proof in appendices, was read on 2026-10-11 from the PostScript file ePrint serves; page numbers below are PDF pages of that file converted with Ghostscript.
sections.heading: Version and bibliographic notes

sections.content: Section 1 (PDF p. 2) asks whether any semantically secure public-key encryption scheme can be used, without further assumptions, to construct a CCA-secure one, calls this one of the major open problems in cryptography, traces its first explicit posing to Bellare et al., and states that no equivalence is known through black-box or non-black-box constructions. This supports chosen-ciphertext security from any CPA-secure encryption. Section 1.2 (PDF pp. 4–5) states the main result informally and Theorem 26 (§4, PDF p. 23) formally: there is no black-box construction of a CCA1-secure scheme from a semantically secure one whose decryption algorithm does not use the encryption algorithm of the underlying scheme. Relative to the same oracle, a CCA2-secure scheme whose decryption does use that encryption algorithm exists, so the restriction is inherent to the proof technique. The concluding section (PDF p. 76) leaves open whether the black-box separation extends to all constructions.

sections.heading: Overview

sections.content: The conference version appears at CRYPTO 2019. The ePrint full version, revised 2021-06-04, adds the leakage-resilience and selective-opening results and the details omitted from the proceedings (§1.4, PDF p. 7); it was read on 2026-10-11. Page numbers are PDF pages; the printed page number is one less.
sections.heading: Version and bibliographic notes

sections.content: Section 1.1 (PDF p. 3) calls the question whether IND-CCA secure public-key encryption can be built from an IND-CPA secure one a major open question in cryptography. Theorem 2 (§4.1, PDF p. 18) proves the KEM of Figure 3 IND-CCA secure if the underlying KEM is IND-CPA secure and almost-all-keys correct, the secret-key encryption is one-time KDM secure for projection functions, whose output bits each depend on at most one key bit (Definition 6, PDF p. 15), and the hash is target collision resistant. Corollary 1 (PDF p. 18) turns this into a fully black-box construction of IND-CCA encryption from IND-CPA encryption and such secret-key encryption with plaintexts of length Ω(n·λ) for key length n, and Corollary 2 into one from projection-KDM-secure public-key encryption alone. These settle PKE-OP-014 and give the theorem behind PKE-OP-015. Decapsulation re-runs the encapsulation algorithm of the underlying KEM, and Theorem 4 (§5, PDF p. 29) shows that no black-box construction from projection-KDM-secure encryption whose decryption avoids this reaches even IND-CCA1 security. Theorem 3 (PDF pp. 18-19) builds one-time projection-KDM secure secret-key encryption from a hinting PRG. Theorems 7 and 8 (§6.1, PDF p. 34) extend the construction to trapdoor functions with adaptive one-wayness, which with earlier results gives one from sub-exponentially hard constant-noise LPN (PDF p. 35).

historical_context.narrative: The public-key concept still needed a concrete way for strangers to establish shared key material. Diffie and Hellman supplied an interactive exchange: each participant publishes an exponentiation, then combines the received value with a private exponent to reach the same group element. The protocol became a durable primitive for session-key establishment and later underlay ElGamal and DHKEM constructions. It is intentionally not called PKE in this atlas. Both parties contribute messages, and the original exchange does not by itself authenticate their identities or encrypt an arbitrary plaintext for an offline recipient.
historical_context.prior_boundary: Parties without a pre-shared secret lacked a public-channel procedure for deriving fresh common key material from independently chosen private values.
historical_context.significance_at_publication: The protocol became a foundation for later ElGamal masking and DH-based KEM suites, but key agreement itself remained distinct from noninteractive public-key encryption.
historical_context.technical_delta: The exponential key exchange let both participants compute the same group element from public messages and their own secret exponent.

limitations: Key agreement is not a complete PKE, KEM ciphertext interface, or authenticated channel.
qualifiers: Interactive unauthenticated key agreement in the paper's cyclic-group setting.

historical_context.narrative: Before 1976, encryption generally began with a secret that sender and receiver had somehow exchanged securely. Diffie and Hellman proposed a different architecture: some keying information could be published without disclosing the private capability needed to reverse or authenticate an operation. That change defined the public-key research program and made open distribution of enciphering material a legitimate cryptographic interface. It was a concept and feasibility agenda, not yet a complete public-key encryption algorithm; RSA, ElGamal, and code-based constructions later supplied distinct concrete realizations.
historical_context.prior_boundary: Conventional cryptography assumed that communicating parties first shared the same secret, making key distribution part of the trusted channel problem.
historical_context.significance_at_publication: This conceptual separation created the research program for public-key encryption and signatures, while leaving concrete trapdoor constructions as an explicit open direction.
historical_context.technical_delta: The paper proposed an asymmetric interface with publicly distributable information and separately held secret information.

limitations: The contribution does not by itself instantiate secure PKE, a KEM, or an authenticated protocol.
qualifiers: Conceptual public-key interface rather than one concrete encryption algorithm.

historical_context.narrative: RSA and Diffie–Hellman made public-key cryptography concrete through number theory, but they did not exhaust the possible hardness foundations. McEliece instead published a disguised generator matrix and encrypted a codeword after injecting a correctable error. The secret algebraic code made decryption efficient while generic decoding remained hard. This was a complete PKE construction rather than a key-agreement protocol, and its source of asymmetry was qualitatively different from modular inversion or discrete logarithms. The historical scheme is not automatically a modern CCA KEM; any later profile needs its own transform, parameters, security statement, and evidence.
historical_context.prior_boundary: The first public-key agenda was dominated by number-theoretic trapdoors and did not establish that error-correcting codes could support an asymmetric encryption interface.
historical_context.significance_at_publication: The construction established that public-key encryption could rest on hard decoding rather than a number-theoretic trapdoor, opening an independent construction branch.
historical_context.technical_delta: McEliece hid an efficiently decodable algebraic code behind public linear transformations and used intentional decoding errors as ciphertext randomization.

limitations: The original construction is not a modern CCA-secure KEM or a current normative profile.
qualifiers: Historical PKE under the paper's code and error parameters.

historical_context.narrative: The public-key agenda required an algorithm that anyone could apply in the forward direction while only one key holder could efficiently reverse it. RSA provided that algebraic relation through modular exponentiation and a secret inverse exponent derived from the modulus factors. A sender could now encrypt for an offline recipient using only published material. The root is historically decisive but cryptographically narrow: textbook RSA is deterministic and structurally malleable, so it does not satisfy modern indistinguishability notions. OAEP belongs later in the lineage precisely because secure deployment requires randomized encoding and rejection behavior around this permutation.
historical_context.prior_boundary: Diffie and Hellman had articulated public-key cryptography while leaving an efficient general trapdoor construction as a central unresolved problem.
historical_context.significance_at_publication: The result made noninteractive public-key encryption concrete and created the trapdoor-permutation branch later wrapped by randomized encodings such as OAEP.
historical_context.technical_delta: RSA instantiated that interface with modular exponentiation whose inverse is efficiently available to the holder of the factorization-derived secret exponent.

limitations: Textbook RSA is deterministic and not IND-CPA or CCA secure.

historical_context.narrative: Diffie–Hellman let two active participants derive a common group element, but it was not an offline-recipient encryption algorithm. ElGamal turned the same ephemeral-exponent idea into PKE: the ciphertext carries a fresh public group element and uses the corresponding shared value to mask the message under a long-term recipient key. Randomization distinguished it from textbook RSA and supported a clean CPA-security account in suitable groups. Its multiplicative structure also made ciphertexts malleable, so the construction remains the starting point—not the endpoint—for the later standard-model CCA design of Cramer and Shoup.
historical_context.prior_boundary: Diffie–Hellman established interactive shared-secret derivation, while RSA supplied deterministic noninteractive encryption through a trapdoor permutation.
historical_context.significance_at_publication: The construction became the standard discrete-log PKE baseline whose algebraic malleability later Cramer–Shoup hardened against adaptive ciphertext attacks.
historical_context.technical_delta: ElGamal converted the ephemeral shared group value into randomized noninteractive encryption under a recipient's long-term public key.

limitations: ElGamal is malleable and does not provide chosen-ciphertext security.
qualifiers: Randomized PKE in an appropriate cyclic group.

historical_context.narrative: RSA's trapdoor relation made public-key encryption possible, but applying it directly to a message leaked equality and preserved unwanted algebraic structure. OAEP inserted a randomized two-hash encoding before the permutation and required structured recovery during decoding. That design made encoding and rejection part of the cryptographic construction rather than application folklore. The 1994 paper claimed strong random-oracle security for the enhanced scheme, but later work exposed a gap in the generic proof and established narrower results for particular instantiations such as RSA-OAEP. This node therefore records the transform and its security program, not a blanket IND-CCA theorem for every trapdoor permutation.
historical_context.prior_boundary: Raw trapdoor-permutation encryption was deterministic and exposed algebraic structure, preventing it from meeting modern ciphertext-security goals.
historical_context.significance_at_publication: The transform established a practical randomized-encoding program around trapdoor permutations, but the original generic chosen-ciphertext claim was not the final security boundary for every instantiation.
historical_context.technical_delta: OAEP added randomized masking, redundancy, and a decoding validity boundary around the permutation input.

limitations: The original generic proof does not by itself establish IND-CCA security for every trapdoor-permutation instantiation; this caveat is checked against Shoup, OAEP Reconsidered, Abstract and Sections 1–2 (IACR ePrint 2000/060).
qualifiers: Random-oracle transform for a trapdoor permutation; theorem scope is instantiation-sensitive.

historical_context.narrative: ElGamal ciphertexts could be modified algebraically, so a decryption oracle gave an attacker leverage unavailable in the CPA game. Cramer and Shoup changed the ciphertext structure by adding group components and hashing them into a consistency exponent checked during decryption. A malformed or recombined ciphertext would normally fail before revealing a plaintext. This construction mechanism is recorded separately from its security theorem: the equation explains how the design works, while the companion node states the adaptive CCA guarantee and assumptions that make the hardening claim meaningful.
historical_context.prior_boundary: ElGamal achieved randomized CPA encryption but allowed algebraic ciphertext modifications that an adaptive decryption oracle could expose.
historical_context.significance_at_publication: This architecture supplied a practical standard-model route to CCA security rather than relying only on generic random-oracle encodings.
historical_context.technical_delta: The construction bound ciphertext components together through a target-collision-resistant hash and rejected values failing the consistency relation.

limitations: The consistency mechanism alone is not a generic compiler for arbitrary PKE.
qualifiers: ElGamal-like discrete-log construction with an explicit rejection check.

historical_context.narrative: Chosen-ciphertext security had been an important target, but efficient constructions commonly relied on random-oracle encodings or remained vulnerable to adaptive decryption queries. Cramer and Shoup proved that their consistency-checked discrete-log scheme reaches the stronger game in the standard model under the paper's exact assumptions. The result changed the accepted feasibility boundary for practical PKE. It is kept apart from the ciphertext architecture because a construction diagram is not a theorem: the security node owns the adversary model and reduction, while the companion node owns the algebraic checking mechanism.
historical_context.prior_boundary: Earlier practical PKE either stopped at chosen-plaintext security or obtained stronger guarantees through idealized random-oracle encodings.
historical_context.significance_at_publication: The theorem established a landmark standard-model CCA point and made proof model a first-class coordinate in comparing hardened public-key encryption.
historical_context.technical_delta: The proof showed that the hash-bound ciphertext consistency design resists adaptive decryption queries without programming a random oracle.

limitations: The theorem applies to the exact Cramer–Shoup construction and assumptions, not all ElGamal variants.
qualifiers: Adaptive CCA security in the paper's standard-model group setting.

historical_context.narrative: Hybrid encryption was efficient, but simply placing a symmetric ciphertext beside a public-key ciphertext did not guarantee security against active decryption queries. Fujisaki and Okamoto tied the components together by hashing message-dependent values into encryption coins and key material, then checking the recovered value by re-encryption. This yielded an IND-CCA hybrid construction under the paper's random-oracle conditions. Kyber later adapted the validation pattern to a KEM, but that later interface should not be projected backward onto the 1999 scheme. The name “FO” now covers several descendants with different rejection rules, assumptions, and quantum-random-oracle analyses.
historical_context.prior_boundary: Efficient hybrid encryption needed a principled way to combine a weaker asymmetric primitive with fast symmetric processing without losing security against active ciphertext attacks.
historical_context.significance_at_publication: FO created the reusable CCA-hardening lineage later instantiated in module-lattice KEMs, while leaving exact variants and proof models construction-specific.
historical_context.technical_delta: The transform coupled asymmetric encryption and symmetric protection through message-dependent hashing and a re-encryption consistency check.

limitations: Later FO-family KEM transforms differ in validation, rejection, assumptions, and proof model.
qualifiers: Generic hybrid transform in the paper's random-oracle treatment.

historical_context.narrative: Once the base HPKE stack was defined, applications still differed in how they authenticated the sender or incorporated an existing shared secret. RFC 9180 addressed that variation through four setup modes: base, PSK, authenticated, and authenticated-PSK. Each mode feeds different credential material into the same labeled schedule and therefore changes the protocol's trust contract. This is a separate capability contribution from the generic KEM-KDF-AEAD composition. An authenticated mode relies on the selected KEM's authentication interface and does not replace application-level identity validation or make every HPKE suite equivalent.

historical_context.narrative: Hybrid public-key encryption is a stack rather than one algorithm: an asymmetric mechanism establishes secret material, a KDF binds context, and an AEAD protects payloads. RFC 9180 standardized how those pieces fit together through labeled extraction, suite identifiers, setup functions, and sender/receiver contexts. This eliminated a class of incompatible ad hoc compositions while allowing several registered component choices. HPKE is therefore represented as a protocol framework, not a KEM row. Its guarantees remain suite- and mode-dependent, and the classical DHKEM registry in the RFC does not make the framework inherently post-quantum.
historical_context.prior_boundary: Applications had many ad hoc ways to combine public-key key establishment with symmetric encryption, creating incompatible context binding, key schedules, and ciphertext formats.
historical_context.significance_at_publication: The framework made hybrid composition interoperable across suites without defining one new KEM or claiming that all component combinations have identical security.
historical_context.technical_delta: HPKE standardized component interfaces, suite identifiers, labeled derivation, setup APIs, and encrypted-message contexts around KEM, KDF, and AEAD choices.

limitations: HPKE is not one KEM, one concrete ciphertext format across all suites, or inherently post-quantum.

metadata.status: As of 2026-10-10 DDH is believed hard in prime-order elliptic-curve groups without an efficient pairing and in prime-order subgroups of finite fields; it is false in groups with a symmetric pairing and in full groups \( \mathbb{Z}_p^* \), and it is broken in quantum polynomial time by Shor's algorithm.

sections.content:
Let \( \mathbb{G} = \langle g \rangle \) be a cyclic group of prime order
\( p \). The DDH assumption states that no probabilistic polynomial-time
algorithm distinguishes

\[
(g, g^{a}, g^{b}, g^{ab}) \quad \text{from} \quad (g, g^{a}, g^{b}, g^{c})
\]

for uniform \( a, b, c \in \mathbb{Z}_p \) with non-negligible advantage. In the
matrix Diffie-Hellman framework DDH is the case \( k = 1 \) of k-Lin.
sections.heading: Definition

sections.content:
DDH fails whenever a group has extra structure that tests the relation: in the
full group \( \mathbb{Z}_p^* \) the Legendre symbol leaks whether exponents are
even, so DDH is used in prime-order subgroups; in groups with an efficiently
computable symmetric pairing \( e(g^a, g^b) = e(g, g^{ab}) \) tests the tuple,
so DDH is easy while CDH may remain hard (Joux and Nguyen 2003). In
prime-order elliptic-curve groups without an efficient pairing, and in the
source groups of asymmetric (Type III) pairings, no attack better than
computing discrete logarithms is known. Boneh's 1998 survey credits Brands
(1993) with observing that earlier undeniable-signature proposals implicitly
relied on DDH.
sections.heading: Status

sections.content:
DDH implies CDH and hence DL. It implies k-Lin for every \( k \ge 1 \)
in the same group, in particular DLIN; the converse fails
in groups with symmetric pairings, where DLIN is believed to hold but DDH does
not. SXDH is DDH in both source groups of an asymmetric pairing.
ElGamal (`PKE-PAPER-1985-ELGAMAL`) and Cramer-Shoup (`PKE-PAPER-1998-CS`)
encryption, TreePIR (`[LP23b]`) and the Glacius threshold
Schnorr signature (`[BDLR24]`) rely on DDH.

metadata.status: As of 2026-10-10 no practical attack on Classic McEliece parameters is known, but a 2026 preprint gives a quasipolynomial-time distinguisher between Goppa codes and random codes in the Classic McEliece regime, with heuristic decryption and key-recovery attacks of the same asymptotic cost, and another 2026 preprint gives a key-recovery attack that solves published challenge instances but stays above the targeted security levels.

sections.content:
Let \( \mathcal{G} \) be a binary Goppa code of length \( n \), dimension
\( k \ge n - mt \) and error-correcting capability \( t \), defined by an
irreducible polynomial of degree \( t \) over \( \mathbb{F}_{2^m} \) and a
support of \( n \) field elements. The public key is a generator (or
parity-check) matrix \( G_{\mathrm{pub}} \) of \( \mathcal{G} \) in a form that
hides its algebraic structure (originally \( S G P \) with random invertible
\( S \) and permutation \( P \); in Classic McEliece, systematic form). The
McEliece problem is: given \( G_{\mathrm{pub}} \) and \( y = x G_{\mathrm{pub}} + e \)
with \( e \) of Hamming weight \( t \), recover \( x \) (equivalently \( e \)).

Security is usually argued from two assumptions together: (i) public
Goppa-code matrices are indistinguishable from uniformly random matrices, and
(ii) decoding \( t \) errors in a random linear code (syndrome decoding) is
hard.
sections.heading: Definition

sections.content:
Decoding general linear codes is NP-hard in the worst case (Berlekamp, McEliece
and van Tilborg 1978), and information-set decoding of random codes remains
exponential in \( t \) at the rates used. For Goppa codes, Faugère et al. (2011)
distinguished public keys from random matrices only at rates close to 1,
outside the parameters of the encryption scheme. In 2026 two preprints changed
this picture: Ghoshal, Ishai, Jain and Sun (ePrint 2026/1630) give a provable
distinguisher running in time \( n^{O(\log n)} \) in the Classic McEliece
regime \( m = \Theta(\log n) \), \( t = \Theta(n/\log n) \), which they state
covers all Classic McEliece parameter sets considered by NIST, together with
heuristic decryption and key-recovery attacks of the same asymptotic cost;
they report improved but not yet practical concrete estimates. Hemmert
(ePrint 2026/1339) gives a key-recovery attack based on higher-order vanishing
that solves previously unbroken challenge instances and conjectures a cost for
Classic McEliece that is still well above the targeted security levels. Both
are preprints as of 2026-10-10.

In March 2025 NIST selected HQC rather than Classic McEliece as the additional
code-based KEM to standardize (NIST IR 8545).
sections.heading: Status

sections.content:
The assumption is not known to be implied by, or to imply, any lattice
assumption. Assumption (i) above is the part affected by the
2026 distinguisher; assumption (ii), hardness of decoding random linear codes,
is not. The scheme of `PKE-PAPER-1978-MCELIECE` and its Niederreiter dual rely
on the same problem.

metadata.status: As of 2026-10-10 no attack on Module-LWE with the parameters of ML-KEM (FIPS 203) or ML-DSA (FIPS 204), both published on 13 August 2024, is known to beat generic lattice reduction.

sections.content:
Let \( R = \mathbb{Z}[x]/(x^n + 1) \) (or another ring of integers of degree
\( n \)), \( R_q = R/qR \), and let \( d \ge 1 \) be the module rank. For a
secret \( s \in R_q^{d} \), a sample is

\[
(a, \; b = \langle a, s \rangle + e) \in R_q^{d} \times R_q, \qquad a \leftarrow R_q^{d},\; e \leftarrow \chi ,
\]

with \( \chi \) a narrow error distribution on \( R \) (in ML-KEM, a centered
binomial distribution). Search Module-LWE asks for \( s \); decision Module-LWE
asks to distinguish samples from uniform. With \( d = 1 \) this is Ring-LWE; with \( n = 1 \) and \( R = \mathbb{Z} \) it is LWE in
dimension \( d \).
sections.heading: Definition

sections.content:
Langlois and Stehlé (2015) gave worst-case to average-case reductions for
module lattices, from approximate SVP on module lattices of rank \( d \) to
Module-LWE (quantum) and to Module-SIS (classical). Module-LWE is the hardness
assumption of ML-KEM (`PKE-PAPER-2024-FIPS203`, derived from
`PKE-PAPER-2017-KYBER`) and, together with Module-SIS, of ML-DSA
(`[NIST24/FIPS204]`, derived from `[DKL+18]`). Concrete
security of these parameter sets is estimated by primal and dual lattice
attacks, treating the module structure as giving no extra advantage; no
algebraic attack exploiting the module structure is known for these rings.
sections.heading: Status

sections.content:
Module-LWE interpolates between LWE and Ring-LWE. Brakerski, Gentry and
Vaikuntanathan (2012) had already defined a general LWE problem (GLWE)
covering both, without studying the intermediate ranks. Module-LWE with
matching parameters implies Module-SIS by the same argument as for
LWE and SIS. Hint-MLWE, which reveals additional noisy linear
information about the secret, implies Module-LWE trivially and is reduced to
Module-LWE for suitable parameters by its authors.

metadata.name: Random oracle model (ROM)

references.citation: Mihir Bellare and Phillip Rogaway, Random Oracles are Practical: A Paradigm for Designing Efficient Protocols, ACM CCS 1993

metadata.status: As of 2026-10-10 the random oracle heuristic is not known to fail for any natural scheme in wide use, but there are artificial schemes that are secure in the ROM and insecure under every concrete hash function (Canetti, Goldreich, Halevi 1998).

sections.content:
A proof in the random oracle model gives every party, honest or adversarial,
oracle access to a uniformly random function
\( H : \{0,1\}^* \to \{0,1\}^{\ell} \) (or to a random function into a group or
another range). The reduction may observe the adversary's oracle queries and
choose the answers ("programming"), as long as the answers are distributed
uniformly. A scheme is then deployed with \( H \) replaced by a concrete hash
function such as SHA-2 or SHA-3. The model is a heuristic: it is not a
hardness assumption about any concrete function.

In the quantum random oracle model (QROM) the adversary may query \( H \) in
superposition, which is the appropriate model when the adversary is quantum
and \( H \) is a public hash function.
sections.heading: Definition

sections.content:
Canetti, Goldreich and Halevi constructed signature and encryption schemes that
are secure in the random oracle model but insecure for every efficiently
computable instantiation of the oracle. Their schemes are artificial; no
comparable failure is known for natural schemes such as RSA-OAEP
(`PKE-PAPER-1994-OAEP`), Fiat-Shamir signatures (`[FS86]`) or the
Fujisaki-Okamoto transform (`PKE-PAPER-1999-FO`) when instantiated with
standard hash functions. Because the instantiation claim is not a
statement about a fixed computational problem, it is not falsifiable in the
usual sense.

Classical ROM proofs that rewind the adversary or inspect its queries do not
automatically carry over to quantum adversaries; Boneh et al. (2011)
introduced the QROM for that reason, and many Fiat-Shamir and
Fujisaki-Okamoto results have since been re-proved there.
sections.heading: Status

sections.content:
The ROM is often combined with a concrete assumption (for example RSA with
random oracles for OAEP, ASM-RSA; or generic groups with random oracles,
Generic group model (GGM), including the generic bilinear group model). A security proof "in the ROM under assumption X" assumes both the
idealized hash function and the hardness of X; it says nothing about security
with a concrete hash function beyond the heuristic.

metadata.status: As of 2026-10-10 no way to invert RSA with properly generated keys is known other than factoring the modulus; it is broken in quantum polynomial time by Shor's algorithm, and it is open whether RSA is as hard as factoring.

sections.content:
Let \( N = pq \) be a product of two random primes of equal length and let
\( e \) be an exponent with \( \gcd(e, \varphi(N)) = 1 \) (fixed small values
such as \( e = 65537 \), or random). The RSA assumption states that, given
\( (N, e) \) and a uniformly random \( y \in \mathbb{Z}_N^* \), no
probabilistic polynomial-time algorithm computes \( x \) with

\[
x^{e} \equiv y \pmod N
\]

with non-negligible probability. The function \( x \mapsto x^e \bmod N \) is a
permutation of \( \mathbb{Z}_N^* \) with trapdoor \( d = e^{-1} \bmod \varphi(N) \).
sections.heading: Definition

sections.content:
Factoring \( N \) breaks RSA, and no better general attack is known; Integer factorization (factoring)
describes the current factoring frontier and
Shor's quantum algorithm. Whether RSA inversion is as hard as factoring is
open: Boneh and Venkatesan (1998) show that for small \( e \) an algebraic
reduction from factoring is unlikely, while Aggarwal and Maurer (2009) show
that breaking RSA with generic ring algorithms is equivalent to factoring.
Attacks on key generation choices, such as a small private exponent
\( d < N^{0.292} \) (Wiener 1990; Boneh and Durfee 1999), or on unpadded use
with small \( e \), concern parameter or usage choices rather than the
assumption itself.
sections.heading: Status

sections.content:
RSA implies factoring and gives a candidate trapdoor permutation (ASM-TDP).
Strong RSA, where the adversary may choose the exponent,
implies RSA. RSA-OAEP (`PKE-PAPER-1994-OAEP`), RSA-PSS (`[BR96]`)
and Shoup's threshold RSA (`[Shoup00]`) are proven secure from RSA
in the random oracle model (ASM-ROM).

metadata.status: As of 2026-10-10 the standard instantiations (RSA, Rabin squaring) are believed secure classically but are broken by Shor's algorithm, and no widely accepted post-quantum trapdoor permutation is known.

sections.content:
A family of trapdoor permutations consists of efficient algorithms
\( \mathsf{Gen}, \mathsf{Eval}, \mathsf{Inv} \): \( \mathsf{Gen}(1^\lambda) \)
outputs an index \( i \) and a trapdoor \( t \); \( f_i = \mathsf{Eval}(i, \cdot) \)
is a permutation of a domain \( D_i \) that can be sampled uniformly; and
\( \mathsf{Inv}(t, \cdot) = f_i^{-1} \). The assumption is that such a family
exists and is one-way: for uniform \( x \in D_i \), no probabilistic
polynomial-time algorithm given \( (i, f_i(x)) \) outputs \( x \) with
non-negligible probability.

This is a generic assumption about the existence of a primitive; concrete
schemes instantiate it with a specific family.
sections.heading: Definition

sections.content:
The RSA function (ASM-RSA) and Rabin's squaring function on quadratic residues
modulo a Blum integer (one-way if factoring, Integer factorization (factoring), is hard) are the
standard instantiations; both are broken in quantum polynomial time. Lattice
trapdoors give trapdoor functions that are not permutations, and no widely
accepted post-quantum trapdoor permutation is known, which is why the
post-quantum status is left as not applicable.
sections.heading: Status

sections.content:
RSA, factoring (via Rabin's function) and claw-free permutation pairs each imply that trapdoor permutations exist. Bellare and
Rogaway prove OAEP (`PKE-PAPER-1994-OAEP`) semantically secure for any
trapdoor permutation in the random oracle model (ASM-ROM).

sections.content:
A public-key encryption (PKE) scheme has three algorithms. KeyGen outputs a
public key and a secret key. Enc encrypts a message under the public key, and
Dec recovers it with the secret key. A key encapsulation mechanism (KEM)
replaces Enc and Dec by Encaps, which outputs a ciphertext together with a
fresh shared key, and Decaps, which recovers that key from the ciphertext.
Correctness may hold only with overwhelming probability: lattice- and
code-based schemes have a small decryption-failure probability. Security asks
that ciphertexts hide the message, or that the encapsulated key look random,
under chosen-plaintext or chosen-ciphertext attack. The public-key idea comes
from PKE-PAPER-1976-DH, which gave interactive key agreement rather than
encryption.
sections.heading: What it is

sections.content:
- **IND-CPA**: an adversary that picks two messages cannot tell which one a
  challenge ciphertext encrypts. This indistinguishability notion and semantic
  security go back to PKE-PAPER-1984-GM. Encryption must be randomized:
  deterministic schemes such as textbook RSA (PKE-PAPER-1978-RSA) cannot be
  IND-CPA.
- **IND-CCA1 and IND-CCA2**: the adversary also gets a decryption oracle,
  before the challenge only (CCA1) or also afterwards on every ciphertext
  except the challenge (CCA2, adaptive chosen-ciphertext attack). IND-CCA2
  implies non-malleability. ElGamal (PKE-PAPER-1985-ELGAMAL) is IND-CPA under
  DDH but malleable, so not IND-CCA2.
- **KEM/DEM hybrid encryption**: a KEM establishes a key and a symmetric data
  encapsulation mechanism (DEM), typically an AEAD scheme, encrypts the
  message. An IND-CCA KEM combined with a one-time IND-CCA DEM gives an
  IND-CCA hybrid PKE.
- **Proof model**: standard model or random-oracle model (ROM); for
  post-quantum security, the quantum ROM (QROM), where hash queries may be in
  superposition.
- **Fujisaki–Okamoto (FO) transform**: turns a weakly secure PKE into an
  IND-CCA scheme in the ROM by deriving the encryption randomness from a hash
  of the message and re-encrypting during decryption to reject malformed
  ciphertexts (PKE-PAPER-1999-FO). Modern KEM variants split it into a
  derandomization step and a KEM step with explicit or implicit rejection
  (PKE-PAPER-2017-HHK); decryption failures enter the security bound.
- **Post-quantum assumptions**: module-LWE for Kyber and ML-KEM; hardness of
  decoding for code-based schemes such as McEliece (PKE-PAPER-1978-MCELIECE);
  learning parity with noise (LPN), where the noise rate matters.
sections.heading: Core notions

sections.content:
- **Trapdoor permutations with randomized encodings**: RSA
  (PKE-PAPER-1978-RSA) with OAEP padding, whose original ROM
  chosen-ciphertext argument had a generic gap (PKE-PAPER-1994-OAEP).
- **Discrete-logarithm encryption**: ElGamal (PKE-PAPER-1985-ELGAMAL), and a
  practical IND-CCA2 scheme in the standard model under DDH and a hash
  assumption (PKE-PAPER-1998-CS).
- **Code-based encryption**: a disguised decodable code plus a bounded error
  vector (PKE-PAPER-1978-MCELIECE), and LPN-based schemes at low noise
  (PKE-PAPER-2003-ALEKHNOVICH, PKE-PAPER-2014-KMP).
- **Module-lattice KEMs**: Kyber, an FO-type KEM over module-LWE
  (PKE-PAPER-2017-KYBER), standardized with three parameter sets as ML-KEM
  (PKE-PAPER-2024-FIPS203).
- **Hybrid frameworks**: HPKE composes a KEM, a key-derivation function, and
  an AEAD scheme in base, pre-shared-key, authenticated, and
  authenticated-PSK modes (PKE-PAPER-2022-HPKE).
sections.heading: Main approaches

sections.content:
As of 2026-10-10, the post-quantum KEM standard covered here is ML-KEM
(PKE-PAPER-2024-FIPS203), an IND-CCA KEM built from module-LWE through an
FO-type transform with implicit rejection. Classical CCA security is available
both in the standard model from specific assumptions (PKE-PAPER-1998-CS) and
in the ROM through generic transforms (PKE-PAPER-1999-FO), where the reduction
from IND-CPA is tight (PKE-PAPER-2017-HHK). Three questions remain open. First,
[a tight QROM reduction from IND-CPA](PKE-OP-002) for FO KEMs is open: known
reductions lose a square root (PKE-PAPER-2018-JZCWM, PKE-PAPER-2019-BHHHP) or a
polynomial factor in the query depth (PKE-PAPER-2020-KSSSS,
PKE-PAPER-2024-GLX), and reductions that run the adversary once and measure
one oracle query cannot avoid the square root (PKE-PAPER-2021-JZM). Second,
whether [CPA security alone yields CCA security](PKE-OP-010) in the standard
model is open; black-box constructions whose decryption never re-encrypts are
ruled out (PKE-PAPER-2007-GMM, PKE-PAPER-2024-HDV), and known transforms add a
primitive such as KDM-secure secret-key encryption (PKE-PAPER-2019-KMT) or
bound the number of decryption queries (PKE-PAPER-2006-CHK). Third, from LPN
in dimension \(n\), PKE is known at noise rate about \(1/\sqrt{n}\) under
polynomial hardness (PKE-PAPER-2014-KMP) or at constant noise under
sub-exponential hardness (PKE-PAPER-2016-YZ); [constant noise with
polynomial hardness](PKE-OP-001) is open. Hybrid classical/post-quantum KEM
combiners are not yet covered.
sections.heading: Where the frontier is

sections.content:
This topic covers ordinary PKE, KEMs, generic transforms that change
ciphertext security, and hybrid-encryption frameworks, with Diffie–Hellman
key agreement as a foundational neighbour. Attribute-based encryption has its
own topic; identity-based, functional, searchable, proxy, threshold, and
multi-recipient encryption are out of scope.

PKE-RESULT-1976-DH-INTERACTIVE-PUBLIC-CH.label: Interactive DH key agreement
PKE-RESULT-1976-DH-INTERACTIVE-PUBLIC-CH.lane_rationale: Gives the interactive exponential key-agreement protocol, an unauthenticated construction rather than the general public-key notion.
PKE-RESULT-1976-DH-INTERACTIVE-PUBLIC-CH.selection_rationale: This adjacent node prevents “public-key cryptography” from being read as synonymous with PKE; it records an interactive, unauthenticated key-establishment capability later reused by ElGamal and HPKE's DHKEM suites.

PKE-RESULT-1976-DH-PUBLIC-KEY-CRYPTOGRAP.label: Public-key cryptography concept
PKE-RESULT-1976-DH-PUBLIC-KEY-CRYPTOGRAP.lane_rationale: Introduces the public/private cryptographic interface independently of any particular PKE or key-agreement algorithm.
PKE-RESULT-1976-DH-PUBLIC-KEY-CRYPTOGRAP.selection_rationale: Omitting this definition would make the map begin with a particular formula and hide the earlier conceptual shift from shared-secret distribution to a public/private interface.

PKE-RESULT-1978-MCELIECE-CODE-BASED-PUBL.label: McEliece code-based PKE
PKE-RESULT-1978-MCELIECE-CODE-BASED-PUBL.lane_rationale: Constructs encryption from a disguised decodable code and bounded errors; its historical role does not turn the algorithm into a model definition.
PKE-RESULT-1978-MCELIECE-CODE-BASED-PUBL.selection_rationale: McEliece is the seed's independent code-decoding PKE root, first showing that public-key encryption can rest on hard decoding; without it, the early map would incorrectly suggest that public-key encryption developed only from number-theoretic trapdoors.

PKE-RESULT-1978-RSA-RSA-PUBLIC-KEY-ENCRY.label: Textbook RSA encryption root
PKE-RESULT-1978-RSA-RSA-PUBLIC-KEY-ENCRY.lane_rationale: Gives the concrete RSA trapdoor-permutation encryption relation, without attributing IND-CPA or CCA security to textbook RSA.
PKE-RESULT-1978-RSA-RSA-PUBLIC-KEY-ENCRY.selection_rationale: RSA supplies the concrete noninteractive trapdoor-permutation root needed to understand both the feasibility of offline-recipient PKE and why OAEP later wraps the deterministic textbook relation.

PKE-RESULT-1985-ELGAMAL-RANDOMIZED-DISCR.label: Randomized ElGamal PKE
PKE-RESULT-1985-ELGAMAL-RANDOMIZED-DISCR.lane_rationale: Constructs randomized recipient-key encryption from an ephemeral Diffie-Hellman mask, with malleability retained as a limitation.
PKE-RESULT-1985-ELGAMAL-RANDOMIZED-DISCR.selection_rationale: ElGamal connects interactive Diffie–Hellman agreement to randomized recipient-key encryption and provides the malleable algebraic baseline that Cramer–Shoup later hardens.

PKE-RESULT-1994-OAEP-OAEP-RANDOMIZED-ENC.label: OAEP randomized encoding
PKE-RESULT-1994-OAEP-OAEP-RANDOMIZED-ENC.lane_rationale: Provides the randomized two-hash encoding around a trapdoor permutation; its instantiation-sensitive security scope is not a generic CCA theorem.
PKE-RESULT-1994-OAEP-OAEP-RANDOMIZED-ENC.selection_rationale: OAEP marks the move from raw trapdoor permutations to randomized, validity-checked encoding; its inclusion also makes the random-oracle and proof-scope caveat visible instead of treating RSA-OAEP as a generic CCA theorem.

PKE-RESULT-1998-CS-HASH-BOUND-ELGAMAL-CI.label: Hash-bound Cramer–Shoup ciphertexts
PKE-RESULT-1998-CS-HASH-BOUND-ELGAMAL-CI.lane_rationale: Defines the concrete hash-bound ciphertext consistency and rejection mechanism of Cramer-Shoup encryption.
PKE-RESULT-1998-CS-HASH-BOUND-ELGAMAL-CI.selection_rationale: This mechanism node shows how Cramer–Shoup blocks algebraic ciphertext modification through a hash-bound rejection equation, rather than leaving the standard-model CCA theorem unexplained.

PKE-RESULT-1998-CS-STANDARD-MODEL-ADAPTI.label: Standard-model adaptive CCA PKE
PKE-RESULT-1998-CS-STANDARD-MODEL-ADAPTI.lane_rationale: This exact node owns the independently significant standard-model adaptive-CCA theorem, while the companion node owns the concrete consistency-check construction.
PKE-RESULT-1998-CS-STANDARD-MODEL-ADAPTI.selection_rationale: The theorem is the seed's standard-model adaptive-CCA boundary; separating it from the ciphertext mechanism preserves the adversary model and assumptions that make the construction significant.

PKE-RESULT-1999-FO-FUJISAKI-OKAMOTO-CCA-.label: Fujisaki–Okamoto CCA transform
PKE-RESULT-1999-FO-FUJISAKI-OKAMOTO-CCA-.lane_rationale: Provides the reusable random-oracle hybrid-encryption transform with recomputation validation, not every later FO-family KEM variant.
PKE-RESULT-1999-FO-FUJISAKI-OKAMOTO-CCA-.selection_rationale: Fujisaki–Okamoto is the reusable random-oracle hybrid-encryption hardening step later adapted by Kyber; omitting it would make Kyber's re-encryption validation appear construction-specific and historically unmotivated.

PKE-RESULT-2017-KYBER-MODULE-LATTICE-CCA.label: Kyber module-lattice CCA KEM
PKE-RESULT-2017-KYBER-MODULE-LATTICE-CCA.lane_rationale: Constructs the research-version CCA KEM by wrapping its module-lattice CPA component in an FO-family transform, with the reviewed revision named.
PKE-RESULT-2017-KYBER-MODULE-LATTICE-CCA.selection_rationale: Kyber is the module-lattice, FO-transformed research KEM that connects the post-quantum construction line to later standardization; it remains distinct because its 2017 configuration is not FIPS 203 ML-KEM.

PKE-RESULT-2017-KYBER-MODULE-LATTICE-CPA.label: Kyber CPA encryption component
PKE-RESULT-2017-KYBER-MODULE-LATTICE-CPA.lane_rationale: Defines the module-lattice CPA encryption substrate with compression and decryption failures as a component distinct from the full CCA KEM.
PKE-RESULT-2017-KYBER-MODULE-LATTICE-CPA.selection_rationale: This reviewed-related node exposes the CPA encryption substrate, compression, and failure contract underneath Kyber so readers do not mistake the base component for the complete CCA KEM.

PKE-RESULT-2022-HPKE-AUTHENTICATED-AND-P.label: HPKE authentication and PSK modes
PKE-RESULT-2022-HPKE-AUTHENTICATED-AND-P.lane_rationale: Specifies protocol setup variants binding sender credentials and PSKs into the hybrid key schedule; it does not introduce a new KEM or validate application identities.
PKE-RESULT-2022-HPKE-AUTHENTICATED-AND-P.selection_rationale: The additional modes are reviewed separately because sender credentials and PSK inputs change HPKE's trust contract while reusing the same framework; they are not new KEM constructions.

PKE-RESULT-2022-HPKE-KEM-KDF-AEAD-HYBRID.label: HPKE KEM-KDF-AEAD framework
PKE-RESULT-2022-HPKE-KEM-KDF-AEAD-HYBRID.lane_rationale: The RFC-backed claim specifies a concrete suite-parameterized KEM-KDF-AEAD protocol composition, not merely an adoption milestone.
PKE-RESULT-2022-HPKE-KEM-KDF-AEAD-HYBRID.selection_rationale: HPKE changes the comparison object from one KEM to a suite-parameterized KEM–KDF–AEAD protocol interface; without it, the map would conflate encapsulation with complete hybrid message protection.
